q: What does this program print?
code:
from urllib.parse import urlsplit
p = urlsplit('https://site.example/books/find?title=py&page=2#top')
print(p.netloc, p.path, p.query, p.fragment)
why: urlsplit cuts the address into scheme, netloc, path, query and fragment, and the query leaves out the question mark and the fragment the number sign.

q: What does this program print?
why: parse_qs gives a dictionary whose values are lists, so a name that appears twice keeps both values.

q: What does this program print?
why: HTTPStatus(429) is Too Many Requests and HTTPStatus.NOT_FOUND is the integer 404.

q: What does this program print?
code:
import urllib.robotparser as rp
r = rp.RobotFileParser()
r.parse(['User-agent: *', 'Disallow: /a'])
print(r.can_fetch('*', 'https://x.example/a/b'), r.can_fetch('*', 'https://x.example/ab'), r.can_fetch('*', 'https://x.example/b'))
why: The standard-library parser compares the Disallow value as a prefix of the path, so /a/b and /ab are both refused and /b is allowed.

q: What does this program print?
why: The script name is item 0 of sys.argv, so four words give a length of four, and joining the words after it rebuilds the address.

q: What does this program print?
code:
from urllib.parse import quote
print(quote('a b&c/d'))
why: quote writes %20 for a space and %26 for an ampersand, and leaves the slash alone unless safe is set to an empty string.

q: What does this program print?
why: The ok attribute of a response is true for every code below 400, so 204 and 302 count and 403 and 503 do not.

q: What does this program print?
why: An HTTPError prints as HTTP Error followed by the code, a colon and the reason, which is the form of the message raise_for_status gives.

q: What does this program print?
why: The text has one character, and its UTF-8 bytes, which are what a binary file holds, are two.

q: What does this program print?
code:
body = b'x' * 10
print([len(body[i:i + 4]) for i in range(0, len(body), 4)])
why: The chunks have the size asked for except the last, which holds what remains.

q: What does this program print?
why: json.loads turns true into True and null into None, and the outer brackets make a list.

q: What does this program print?
why: Subtracting 273.15 turns Kelvin into Celsius, which gives 37.0.

q: What does this program print?
why: The parser hands the attributes as name and value pairs, and the value of alt is x y.

q: What does this program print?
code: import re print(re.findall(r'', '123'))
why: The pattern needs href right after a, so the tag with a class first is missed.

q: What does this program print?
why: min keeps the smaller of five and the number of links.

q: What does this program print?
code:
urls = ['/a/', '/b/', '#', '/c/']
n = 0
for u in urls:
    if u.endswith('#'):
        break
    n += 1
print(n)
why: The loop stops at the first address that ends in #, after two pages.

q: Which part of a URL comes after the number sign?
why: The optional fragment follows the number sign and the query follows the question mark.

q: Why must a space in a query string be percent-encoded or written as a plus?
options: The server only accepts upper-case letters
Characters such as a space or a comma are not allowed raw in the pairs
A space would end the whole URL and the request would be dropped by Python
Python cannot hold a space inside a string
why: Spaces and commas must be encoded or written as a plus so that the pairs stay readable as name=value.

q: What can a network observer still see when a browser uses HTTPS?
options: What was typed into a form
The name of the site visited
The password sent to the site
why: HTTPS hides the content and the submitted data, but not the name of the site.

q: A response has status 503. Which class of code is it?
why: The first digit gives the class, and 5 means a server error.

q: Why does the comic downloader pause between comics?
options: So that it does not hammer the server with requests
Because Python cannot save two files at once
Because the site asks for a password each time
To let the browser load the images first
why: A crawler that loads many pages pauses so as not to overload the server.

q: What does a site learn from the default user-agent string of requests?
options: The name of the person who runs the script
That the client is a script, python-requests, and not a browser
The operating system of the server
why: requests sends python-requests and its version, which tells a site that the client is a script.

q: What does webbrowser.open return?
options: The status code of the page
True if a browser was launched and False if not
why: webbrowser.open only asks the default browser to show the URL and cannot read the page.

q: What does requests.get return?
why: It returns a Response, which holds the body and the status; the package is installed separately.

q: Which attribute of a Response holds the body as bytes?
why: content holds the bytes and text holds the decoded string.

q: Why do services put a version number such as /geo/1.0/ in an endpoint?
options: So that the key is checked once
So that an old version can be retired without breaking new callers
So that the answer arrives as JSON
So that the request uses HTTPS
why: The version number lets a service retire an old form of the call.

q: Where should a program keep its API key?
options: In the source code, in plain text
In the URL of the web page
In a file the program reads, not in the source code
In the name of the script
why: A key identifies the account and is kept secret, so it is read from a file.

q: A weather call for an unknown city is answered with an empty list. What should the program do?
options: Ask for the same city in Kelvin
Check that the list is not empty before indexing it
why: The call is still answered, so the program checks the shape of the decoded data before indexing it.

q: What is an HTML element?
options: A starting tag, its content and a closing tag
Only the text between two tags
why: Elements are made of the tags and the content between them, and they nest to form the tree of the page.

q: What does requests download from a page that scripts change after it loads?
options: The page as it looks on the screen
The source as the browser first received it, without the later changes
Only the images of the page
The page after the scripts have run
why: The source is the HTML text received, which may differ from the screen.

q: Which key opens the Developer Tools in Firefox, Chrome and Edge?
why: F12 opens them, and Inspect Element shows the tag, id, class and a copy of the CSS selector.

q: In a CSS selector, what does > between two parts mean?
why: A space means any descendant and > means a direct child.

q: What does the second argument of bs4.BeautifulSoup(html, 'html.parser') name?
options: The parser to use, here the one in Python's standard library
The first tag to start from
why: html.parser selects the standard-library parser; the others must be installed.

q: What does select return when nothing matches?
why: select never returns None; select_one does when nothing matches.

q: Which selector matches a p element that has the id author?
why: p#author needs the p element itself to be the author, while p #author needs it inside a p element.

q: How do get_text and str differ on a tag?
options: get_text gives the HTML and str gives the text
get_text gives the text without tags, and str gives the tag's HTML
why: get_text removes the nested tags and turns references such as < back into characters.

q: What does get return for an attribute the tag does not have?
why: get returns None, while attrs is the dictionary of all attributes.

q: Why does the link-verification program turn each href into an absolute URL?
options: Because relative links are always broken
Because many links are relative and cannot be requested as they are
Because requests refuses any http address
Because a 404 only appears for absolute links
why: Relative addresses are resolved against the page URL before they are requested.

q: Why does the chapter's advice about downloading geckodriver differ from current Selenium?
options: Selenium no longer needs a browser
geckodriver is now part of Python
Selenium Manager now finds the driver itself
Selenium only works with Chrome now
why: Selenium Manager ships with Selenium and locates the driver, so no separate download is needed.

q: In Selenium, what kind of value is By.CSS_SELECTOR?
why: The By constants are plain strings such as 'css selector' and 'link text'.

q: Selenium's find_element finds nothing. What happens?
why: find_element raises, while find_elements returns an empty list.

q: Which WebElement attribute gives the rendered text?
why: text gives the rendered text and get_property('innerHTML') gives the source.

q: What does send_keys do?
options: Types into a field or sends a key such as Keys.END
why: click presses, send_keys types, and submit sends the form that contains the element.

q: In which mode does Playwright launch a browser by default?
why: headless=False with slow_mo shows the steps.

q: Which of these returns a Locator in Playwright?
why: A Page offers locators such as get_by_role, get_by_text and locator.

q: A Playwright locator matches seven paragraphs and click() is called on it. What happens?
options: An error is raised, because locators are strict
Nothing happens and None is returned
why: An action on a locator that matches several elements raises an error, so nth picks one.

q: What does Playwright do when a selector matches nothing and an action is asked for?
options: It waits, up to 30 seconds by default, and then fails
why: Auto-waiting makes a mistyped selector pause for the default timeout.

q: A page is built by scripts after it loads. Which approach does the chapter recommend when the service offers one?
options: A regular expression on the HTML
why: An API is preferable whenever the service offers one, and a browser driver is the fallback.

q: Which three things are the ground under every tool of the chapter?
options: Addresses, the protocol and the manners of a visiting program
why: The chapter's tools all rest on how addresses are written, how the protocol answers and how a program should behave on a site.

q: In a URL, what does the part after the question mark hold?
options: A list of names and values
why: The query is a list of name=value pairs and urllib.parse reads it.

q: Which two parts of the protocol do the chapter's programs rely on?
why: HTTPS protects the content in transit and the status codes tell whether a request worked.

q: What does a program that visits a site owe the site?
options: A password for every page it loads
A copy of every file it downloads
A browser window for every request
A limit on its rate of requests and attention to what the site asks crawlers to leave alone
why: Politeness means pausing between requests and reading robots.txt.

q: What does the webbrowser module do with a URL?
options: Hands it to the browser the user already has
Downloads the page and parses it
Starts a separate browser engine inside Python
why: It only asks the default browser to show the page.

q: Where does showmap.py read the address from?
options: The command-line arguments, or the clipboard when there are none
The title of the browser tab
why: It joins the arguments or falls back to the clipboard, then opens a search URL.

q: What does requests turn a URL into?
options: A Response that the program can check, read and save
why: The Response holds the status and the body of the download.

q: Does the requests package come with Python?
options: Yes, it is in the standard library
No, but urllib is its only replacement
why: The chapter says to install requests; urllib.request is the standard-library alternative.

q: Name the two checks that tell a program a download worked.
options: The status code, and the exception raised by raise_for_status
The length of the text, and the file name
The user-agent string, and the cookie
The order of the headers, and the encoding
why: status_code equals requests.codes.ok on success and raise_for_status raises on 4xx and 5xx.

q: How is the body of a response saved to a file?
options: In text mode, in one string
why: iter_content gives the chunks and each is written to a file opened for binary writing.

q: What does a web API let a program do?
options: Draw the page in a window
Ask another program for data, most often answered as JSON
Rewrite the HTML of a site
why: The answer is usually JSON, which json.loads decodes.

q: What does an API call URL usually contain?
options: A folder and a file name
A version, a query and a key
why: A call may also be answered with an error, so the answer is checked.

q: What happens to what an API returns before the program uses it?
options: It is decoded from JSON and then converted into the units needed
It is parsed by Beautiful Soup
It is opened in a browser
why: For example Kelvin becomes Celsius after json.loads.

q: What is a web page, as the program receives it?
why: The source and the Developer Tools show that text.

q: HTML is written as what?
options: Elements made of tags, and the tags carry attributes
A single long string without structure
why: Tags nest into the tree of the page and attributes are name-value pairs inside them.

q: How does the programmer find the element to pick on a page?
options: With the page source and the Developer Tools
why: Inspect Element shows the tag, id, class and a copy of the CSS selector.

q: What does the chapter leave to a parser and not to a regular expression?
why: HTML can be written in many equivalent ways that one pattern misses.

q: What does Beautiful Soup turn the text of a page into?
options: Objects from which elements are selected
why: It parses the text into a tree of Tag objects.

q: What two things go into bs4.BeautifulSoup(...)?
options: The page text and the name of a parser
A file name and a timeout
why: The parser name, such as html.parser, selects how the text is read.

q: What does select find elements by?
why: The Tag objects it returns give their text and attributes.

q: Which three things do the chapter's scraping projects put together?
options: requests, a parser and a stop rule
A browser, a key and a clipboard
JSON, a regular expression and a thread
A driver, a locator and a timer
why: They download, parse and stop at a limit or a marker.

q: Which are the chapter's crawling programs?
options: searchpypi.py, downloadXkcdComics.py and the link verification program
why: Each combines downloading, parsing and a stop rule.

q: What do Selenium and Playwright have in common?
options: They parse HTML without a browser
They start a real browser and drive it as a user does
why: The program controls a real browser, which is slower than a download.

q: What does the chapter's Selenium part cover?
options: Writing API keys to a file
Starting a browser, finding elements, reading them, clicking and sending keys
why: It names find_element, text, click and send_keys.

q: What does the chapter's Playwright part cover?
options: Launching a browser, locators, clicking, filling and pressing keys
why: It uses locators such as get_by_role and actions such as click and fill.

q: What decides whether to use requests or a driven browser?
why: A static page is fetched with requests, a page built by scripts needs a driver, and an API is best when there is one.

q: What does a robots.txt file do?
options: It blocks crawlers at the server
It lists the passwords of a site
It asks crawlers not to fetch some paths, but does not enforce it
why: It is a request and not an access control.

q: When does raise_for_status raise?
why: It does nothing for a download that worked and raises an HTTPError for 4xx and 5xx.

q: Why is a downloaded file opened in write binary mode?
options: Because the bytes are the file's content whatever its text encoding
Because text mode cannot open a new file
Because binary mode is faster than text mode
Because requests converts it to binary anyway
why: Writing bytes to a text-mode file raises TypeError.

q: Why does requests advise stream=True with iter_content for a download?
options: So that the download is encrypted
So that the body is not read whole into memory first
So that the status is checked twice
So that the file is compressed
why: Chunks are written one by one, the last one shorter.

q: What does response.json() raise when the body is a challenge page in HTML?
why: Text that is not JSON raises JSONDecodeError.

q: Which constant equals the success status in requests?
why: status_code equals requests.codes.ok on success.

q: What is item 0 of sys.argv?
options: The first word typed after the script name
why: The script name comes first and the words typed after it follow.

q: What does showmap.py use when no address is given on the command line?
options: A fixed address in the code
The last page the browser showed
why: It takes the address from the command line, or from the clipboard when there is none.

q: In which unit does the weather API of the chapter give the temperature by default?
why: The temperature arrives in Kelvin and is converted by program.

q: What does an attribute like id do in a tag?
options: It names a group of elements
why: id names one element and class names a group.

q: Why does the chapter advise a parser instead of a regular expression for HTML?
options: HTML can be written in many equivalent ways that one pattern misses
Regular expressions cannot read a string with angle brackets
A parser is always faster than re
Regular expressions only work on files
why: A pattern that needs href right after a misses an a tag that has a class first.

q: How many tabs does searchpypi.py open when the page has twelve result links?
why: The count is the smaller of five and the number of links.

q: When does the comic downloader stop?
options: When the page has no image
When the prev link ends in # or after ten downloads
why: It follows the link whose rel is prev until one of the two stops applies.

q: Which function of urllib.parse cuts a URL into its parts?
why: urlsplit cuts the address; urljoin resolves a relative one, quote encodes and parse_qs reads a query.

q: What does parse_qs return for each name?
why: The values are lists, because a name may appear more than once.

q: Which module names the status codes and their phrases?
why: http.HTTPStatus names them.
